summary:
SkyShift helps students, educators, and scientists explore the changing infrared sky with real NASA SPHEREx observations. Enter coordinates, load images, and move between dates to investigate motion and possible brightness changes. Two timescales serve stars and brown dwarfs over months, and comets and asteroids over hours.

Its technical core combines median stacking by visit and detector, 16-bit image arrays, and browser-based contrast stretching, image addition, and subtraction. Photometry builds spectra across all six detectors, while motion measurements are compared with ESA Gaia DR3 predictions. Sources, dates, processing methods, uncertainties, and quality limits remain visible. Targeted validation recovered all 60 known asteroids tested at their predicted positions; a public scoreboard reports results and limitations.

Guided investigations use the same real NASA images and measured spectra. Traditional star names connect cultural astronomy with modern observation. Users can flag candidates, vote on classifications, and export evidence for further review. By combining transparent science, interactive visual comparisons, and accessible teaching, SkyShift helps more people understand NASA data and participate in citizen science.
details:
SkyShift is a browser-based platform for exploring time-domain infrared astronomy with real NASA SPHEREx observations. Built for the “Planet X and SPHEREx” challenge, it connects coordinate-based sky exploration, image comparison, quantitative measurements, guided learning, and citizen-science review. Users can investigate nearby stars, brown dwarfs, comets, and asteroids through the same underlying observational data.

The data engine retrieves SPHEREx Level 2 observations through NASA/IPAC IRSA, with HTTP range reads from NASA’s public S3 archive as an alternative data path. Images are reprojected through their World Coordinate System (WCS) onto a common tangent-plane grid, oriented north up and east left. Processing applies NASA quality flags, accounts for zodiacal-light background where available, and levels exposure backgrounds before stacking. The Months mode creates median stacks by observing visit and detector for slow-moving sources; the Hours mode preserves individual exposures for faster objects. Keeping detectors separate reduces confusion between wavelength-dependent appearance and temporal change. Image processing implementation, data retrieval implementation.

Frames reach the browser as 16-bit numerical arrays with scale and offset metadata. The TypeScript frontend reconstructs surface-brightness values and performs linear or inverse-hyperbolic-sine contrast stretching, inversion, image addition, and signed subtraction locally. Shared display limits across comparison frames preserve meaningful differences between dates. This makes image exploration interactive while retaining access to numerical values and missing-data information. Browser image mathematics.

Spectral extraction operates on individual exposures across all six detectors. Each point uses the source’s position at the exposure time and its wavelength from the WCS-WAVE calibration, retaining flux density, uncertainty, detector, date, visit, and saturation information. Clean sources use aperture photometry with a clipped-median local background and aperture correction. Saturated sources and close neighbours receive dedicated wing-photometry or joint-profile fits, with additional uncertainty where appropriate. Measurements that cannot satisfy the quality checks are omitted with an explanation. Photometry and spectrum implementation.

Motion analysis measures centroid displacement between visit stacks, using their median exposure times and quiet reference stars to estimate the empirical positional error. A reported shift requires a source detected at signal-to-noise ≥ 5 in both stacks and additional checks against missing coverage or mismatched sources. Gaia DR3 positions are propagated to the observation dates for comparison, including parallax in the predicted displacement when available. For larger searches, the batch pipeline implements vectorized weighted least-squares astrometry, detector-specific position offsets, systematic corrections, and uncertainty estimates that account for correlated observations. Motion measurement, batch astrometry.

The batch spectral pipeline combines repeated measurements into 102 project-defined wavelength bins spanning 0.75–5.0 μm. It applies quality filtering, outlier rejection, inverse-variance weighting, and uncertainty inflation when measurements disagree. Visit information is retained so spectral interpretation can consider repeatability. Source measurements are stored in Parquet tables for subsequent analysis. Spectral pipeline.

The repository’s current validation records include:

  • Barnard’s Star: a measured displacement of 10.83″ ± 0.36″ over 0.986 years, compared with Gaia’s 10.27″ prediction.
  • Targeted asteroid recovery: 60 of 60 known asteroids recovered, with a median positional offset of 0.77″; the displaced control produced detections in 2 of 300 images.
  • Search-zone recovery: 434 of 457 known-asteroid sessions at V < 16 recovered through mover detection or track-based recovery in the 100-square-degree test zone.
  • Population-scale astrometry: comparison with 209,534 Gaia stars, with proper-motion scatter of 132 and 135 milliarcseconds per year in the two coordinate components.

These are results from defined samples and test regions; the public scoreboard records their methods, controls, and limitations. Current validation data.

The implementation uses Python, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, SEP, Astroquery, and FastAPI for scientific processing and APIs; TypeScript, Vite, Canvas, and Aladin Lite support the frontend. Featured observations load from precomputed static assets, while other coordinates use cached API requests. Guided investigations reuse real NASA images and measured spectra, with source links and processing explanations. Traditional star names connect cultural astronomy with modern observation, while candidate flags, classification votes, and CSV exports give users a practical route into further scientific review.
